title: Marta Kostyuk gets her WTA Finals debut after Elena Rybakina withdraws
subtitle: The Ukrainian, who travelled to California as the first alternate, will open against Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova. They have already met on three surfaces this season; their only hard-court match went to a deciding set.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Marta Kostyuk was already practising at Indian Wells when her job changed on Saturday. The Ukrainian had come to California as the first singles alternate for the WTA Finals. On Sunday she will play the opening match, taking defending champion Elena Rybakina’s place against Linda Noskova of Czechia.

Rybakina withdrew on 7 November, the day before play was due to begin. Tournament organisers gave the reason as a viral illness. In a statement issued by the Women’s Tennis Association, Rybakina said her body was “just not physically ready to compete” and that she would recover at home before the 2027 season.

A year ago, Rybakina was the last player to qualify for the Finals in Riyadh and went on to win without losing a match. This year she was the first to qualify. She won the Australian Open and the US Open, taking the world No. 1 ranking in New York. She has already secured the year-end No. 1 spot. Her absence opens up the championship without putting that distinction back in play.

Kostyuk’s route into the field began long before the withdrawal. She won the Madrid title this spring and broke into the top ten. Tournament director Garbiñe Muguruza told Reuters that Kostyuk, who was training on site while she waited, had earned her opportunity. Both Kostyuk and Noskova arrive with 35 match wins this season, according to the WTA. Neither has played in the Finals before.
Their fourth meeting of the season

In Madrid, Kostyuk beat Noskova on clay on her way to the title. At Wimbledon, Noskova beat Kostyuk in the semifinals and went on to win the championship. Their only hard-court meeting this year was the closest: Noskova won 7–5, 5–7, 6–4 in the fourth round of the US Open. Indian Wells gives Kostyuk another chance on that surface.

“I never had a goal to end at WTA Finals,” Kostyuk said in comments published by the tour on Saturday. By the time she spoke, she had a place in a group that also includes Americans Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula. Unlike at a Grand Slam, a loss on opening day would not send either debutant home. Each player is scheduled to face the other three in her group, and the top two advance to the semifinals.

The difference between travelling as a reserve and taking the court carries a financial stake as well. The WTA has allocated $8 million of the event’s $10 million purse to singles. An undefeated singles champion would earn $3.37 million including participation fees; that figure depends on winning all five matches.

Kostyuk and Noskova are scheduled to start at noon in California on Sunday, 11 p.m. in Kampala. The winner will take a group victory into her next match. The loser will still have a route to the title.
